item.title: An Expandable Library of Solid Polymer Electrolytes for Lithium‐Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Solid‐polymer‐electrolytes (SPEs) offer alternatives to next‐generation solid‐state lithium‐metal batteries, promising advantages in mechanical‐compliance, processability, cost‐effectiveness, and safety. While tremendous efforts have generated diverse SPEs since 1970s, SPE‐practicality remains limited by the trade‐offs among ion‐conductivity, high‐voltage stability, and Li 0 ‐electrolyte compatibility. Here, we establish the first SPE library covering 12 SPEs across five polymer families, which allows us to collect large datasets on chemistry, interfacial, and electrochemical properties that unveil their hidden connections. Correlation analysis of these descriptors reveals binding‐strength between polymer and Li + , subtle variations in polymer molecular structure, and solid‐electrolyte‐interphase composition as dictating factors. Also discovered is that the standard deviation of coulombic‐efficiency rather than its average value governs the battery cycling stability. The SPE library can be rapidly expanded through two structural engineering pathways: grafting diverse functional segments onto backbones and constructing compositionally‐complex SPEs. As a proof‐of‐concept, we fabricate several such SPEs and find improved high‐voltage stability through gradually increasing the complexity of the polymer matrices. A terpolymer‐based acrylates SPE exhibits outstanding Li 0 plating/stripping over 1800 h, stable cycling in LiCoO 2 ||Li battery with 100% capacity retention and an average coulombic‐efficiency of 99.91% ± 0.09% over 100 cycles. This work provides a transformative framework to design the future polymer materials.

item.title: Decoupling Thermodynamic and Kinetic Moisture Instability Reveals a Critical Humidity Threshold for Sodium Thiophosphate Solid Electrolyte (Adv. Energy Mater. 44/2026)
item.description: Moisture Tolerance In article number e71467, Chengcheng Fang and co-workers reveal that moisture stability in Na3PS4 is governed by competition between dehydration and hydrolysis. Under limited moisture exposure, thermal treatment removes absorbed water and largely restores ionic conductivity, whereas severe exposure promotes irreversible hydrolysis. These findings establish a kinetic basis for moisture tolerance and recovery in sulfide solid electrolytes.

item.title: Decoupling Thermodynamic and Kinetic Moisture Instability Reveals a Critical Humidity Threshold for Sodium Thiophosphate Solid Electrolyte
item.description: ABSTRACT Sodium sulfide solid electrolytes are widely regarded as highly moisture‐sensitive, requiring ultralow‐humidity (typically 15–100 ppm) processing that imposes a major cost barrier to solid‐state battery manufacturing. Yet the actual moisture‐stability limit of these materials remains poorly quantified, and the mechanistic origin of degradation, whether thermodynamic or kinetic, is unresolved. Here, using sodium thiophosphate, Na 3 PS 4 , as a model system, we establish a quantitative moisture‐stability framework that decouples thermodynamic and kinetic contributions to apparent instability. Controlled exposure studies across 13%–38% relative humidity, correlated with H 2 S evolution, mass uptake, structural evolution, and ionic conductivity recovery, reveal a critical humidity threshold near 15% relative humidity, below which Na 3 PS 4 undergoes reversible hydration with minimal hydrolysis on the surface, fully recovering its ionic conductivity at 13% relative humidity after brief heat treatment. Density functional theory shows that hydration is thermodynamically favorable (ΔG = −0.76 eV), whereas hydrolysis is kinetically gated by a 1.78 eV activation barrier, rationalizing the unexpected tolerance. By defining a practical humidity‐tolerance window and a reproducible benchmarking protocol, this work provides a transferable foundation for the rational design of moisture‐tolerant sulfide electrolytes toward substantially relaxed humidity requirements for all‐solid‐state battery manufacturing.

item.title: Functional‐Group Engineering for Durable Solid Electrolyte Interphase Toward Aqueous Copper Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Aqueous copper‐based batteries intrinsically suppress hydrogen evolution, offering a safer alternative to zinc systems. However, their practical deployment remains limited by poor Cu 2+ plating/stripping reversibility. Here we report a functional‐group‐guided strategy to in situ construct an organic‐inorganic hybrid solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on Cu electrodes. By comparing electrolytes with and without additives containing fluorine and sulfur, a clear structure‐function relationship is established. Fluorine‐free molecules fail to form a stable SEI, whereas fluorinated additives generate an organic‐rich SEI with moderate benefits. In contrast, the group with both fluorine and sulfur produces a robust organic‐inorganic hybrid SEI with high mechanical modulus (54.7 GPa) and rapid Cu 2+ transport. This hybrid interphase homogenizes interfacial ion flux and markedly improves Cu 2+ reversibility, enabling Cu||Cu cells to cycle more than 2000 h at 5 mA cm −2 and Cu–MnO 2 full cells to retain stable operation over 2200 cycles. The excellent dimensional stability of the pouch cells further underscores their practical promise. This work establishes functional‐group engineering of the SEI for copper‐based aqueous batteries.

item.title: Machine‐Learning‐Potential‐Driven Volcano Relationship in Grain Boundary Amorphicity and Ionic Transport of Antiperovskite Solid Electrolytes
item.description: ABSTRACT Ionic transport in solid‐state electrolytes is governed by interfacial disorder and local chemical environments, yet their microscopic design principles remain challenging because large‐scale interfacial kinetics are simulated using molecular dynamics (MD), where predictive design requires quantum‐level accuracy. Here, we use an actively learned machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) to bridge this scale‐accuracy gap in halide‐tunable antiperovskite solid electrolytes. By varying the local Cl − /Br − ratio and quantifying interfacial amorphicity and ion flux, we identify an MLIP‐driven volcano relationship between structural disorder and ionic transport. Cl‐enriched grain boundaries remain overly ordered, whereas Br − enrichment induces excessive disorder that disrupts migration. Intermediate halide compositions maximize ionic transport through moderately amorphous environments. Guided by this relationship, we design an anion‐engineered grain boundary through selective halide tuning. These results establish controlled anion segregation as a strategy for reducing interfacial resistance and highlight MLIP‐enhanced MD as a predictive framework for transport and disorder engineering in solid‐state materials.

item.title: Tailoring Li/LATP Interface with In Situ Convertible ZrOP Layer for Solid‐State Li Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT NASICON‐type Li 1.3 Al 0.3 Ti 1.7 (PO 4 ) 3 (LATP) has emerged as one of the most promising solid‐state electrolytes owing to its high ionic conductivity, superior air stability, and low cost. However, the application of LATP‐based solid‐state lithium batteries (SSLBs) is hindered by its poor chemical compatibility with Li. Here, a low‐cost and scalable spray‐coating strategy is proposed to construct an amorphous zirconium oxophosphate (ZrOP) interfacial layer on LATP, which physically isolates LATP from Li to prevent the reduction of Ti 4+ species and the formation of a mixed ionic and electronic conductivity layer. Moreover, the ZrOP layer undergoes an in situ reaction with Li, generating a nanocomposite mixture of Li‐ion conductors, including LiZr 2 (PO 4 ) 3 , Li 2 O, Li 8 ZrO 6 , and Li 3 P during cycling. This transformed interlayer maintains intimate contact to facilitate rapid Li‐ion transport. Consequently, the Li/ZrOP‐LATP/Li symmetric cell achieves stable cycling for over 1300 h at 0.1 mA cm −2 with a critical current density of 2.1 mA cm −2 . The resultant Li/ZrOP‐LATP/LiFePO 4 cell delivers a capacity retention of 82% after 480 cycles at 0.5C. This work provides a facile and effective strategy to simultaneously resolve the chemical instability and poor physical contact at the Li/LATP interface, paving the way toward low‐cost and high‐performance SSLBs.

item.title: Interfacial Electronic‐Structural Coupling Suppresses Jahn‐Teller Instability in NASICON Cathode Casting Long Cycling Life
item.description: ABSTRACT NASICON‐type Na 4 VMn(PO 4 ) 3 cathodes possess attractive high‐voltage and structural robustness, yet its application is hindered by the intrinsic instability of Mn 3+ ‐induced Jahn‐Teller distortion. A mosaic‐like Na 4 VMn(PO 4 ) 3 /NaFePO 4 (NVMP/NFP) heterostructure is constructed to achieve interfacial electronic‐structural synergistic regulation. The nanoscale heterointerfaces induce charge redistribution and modify the local electronic environment, thereby strengthening Mn─O interactions indirectly and interrupting the spatial correlation of local distortions, which successfully suppresses the Jahn‐Teller instability. The suppression of local electronic instability by the NVMP/NFP heterostructure is confirmed by complementary experimental and theoretical analyses, which further reveal reversible V 3+ /V 4+ and Mn 2+ /Mn 3+ redox reactions. Furthermore, the heterointerface reconstructs the Na + transport network by generating more interconnected and multidimensional migration pathways with reduced diffusion barriers, mitigates the accumulation of lattice strain during Na + extraction/insertion and fosters electron transfer, casting fast reversible electrochemical reaction. Benefiting from this interfacial electronic‐structural coupling, the optimized NVMP/NFP cathode delivers excellent wide‐temperature cycling stability, retaining 89.91% capacity after 6000 cycles at 2 A g −1 , 91.80% after 2500 cycles at ‐15°C, and 80.23% after 6000 cycles at 45°C. This work provides an interfacial engineering strategy for decoupling electronic instability from structural degradation and offers a general pathway for stabilizing Jahn‐Teller active electrode materials.

item.title: Function‐Decoupled Dual‐Anion Doping via Site‐Preferential Regulation Enables High‐Performance Lithium Argyrodite Electrolytes
item.description: ABSTRACT All‐solid‐state lithium metal batteries adopting argyrodite‐type sulfide solid‐state electrolytes (SSEs) offer enhanced safety and energy density, yet face challenges in balancing ionic conductivity, air stability and interfacial compatibility. Herein, we pioneer a precursor‐directed site‐preferential dual‐anion doping strategy to address these trade‐offs. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal the oxygen precursor dictates the predominant anion occupancy: Li 2 O kinetically favors O at the 4d sites, whereas P 2 O 5 preferentially directs O to the 16e sites. Guided by this principle, Li 6 PS 4.2 O 0.4 Se 0.4 Cl (LPSOSeCl) SSEs is designed, wherein O preferentially enriches 16e sites to enhance air stability and widen the electrochemical window for high‐voltage cathode compatibility, whereas Se preferentially enriches 4d sites to compensate ionic conductivity and promote a Li 2 Se/Li 2 O‐rich interphase for dendrite suppression. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations combined with radial distribution functions (RDFs) further reveal that the Se/O co‐doping facilitates the formation of a stable Li/SSE interface, significantly inhibiting LPSOSeCl SSE reduction. The resulting LPSOSeCl SSE achieves high ionic conductivity, excellent moist air stability and remarkable critical current density (CCD) of 2.6 mA cm −2 . The Li||Li symmetric cells demonstrate ultralong cycling stability over 4000 h at 0.2 mA cm −2 and LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 full cells rentain 70.7% capacity retention after 500 cycles at 0.3C.

item.title: Hierarchically Porous Unsubstituted Olefin‐Linked COF With Synergistically Enhanced Electronic and Ionic Conductivities for High‐Performance Lithium‐Ion Battery Cathodes
item.description: ABSTRACT The development of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) with synergistically enhanced ionic/electronic conductivities, improved active site utilization, and increased chemical stability for achieving high‐performance lithium–ion battery (LIB) cathodes remain a significant challenge. Here, we report the rational design of a novel unsubstituted olefin–linked, highly crystalline COF (namely HATN–ICTO COF) as a cathode for LIBs. The HATN–ICTO COF integrates extended fully conjugated π–networks, hierarchical porosity, and dual redox–active centers, enabling a synergistic improvement in ionic and electronic conductivity as well as a high theoretical capacity. This unique unsubstituted olefin linkage also endows the COF with excellent chemical stability, thereby ensuring long‐term cycling performance. Meanwhile, the hierarchical porous architecture of the COF can effectively buffer the volume expansion during repeated charge–discharge processes, mitigating electrode damage. The COF delivers a high specific capacity of 293 mAh g − 1 at 0.1 A g − 1 and maintains 206 mAh g − 1 at 10.0 A g − 1 , with outstanding cycling performance of 155 mAh g − 1 at 5.0 A g − 1 after 18,000 cycles. Additionally, a pouch cell based on the HATN–ICTO COF//Li configuration was also demonstrated. This work provides fundamental insights into structure–property relationships governing charge delocalization and redox activity in COFs.

item.title: Al/F Co‐Doped Sulfide Electrolyte for Durable All‐Solid‐State Lithium‐Organic Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Carbonyl‐containing organic cathodes offer a sustainable route to high‐energy storage, but their reaction with conventional sulfide electrolytes (SEs) causes interfacial degradation in all‐solid‐state lithium‐metal batteries (ASSLMBs). Here we develop an electrolyte‐first strategy that stabilizes both carbonyl cathodes and lithium metal through dual‐site Al/F substitution of an argyrodite SE, Li 5.7 Al 0.1 P 0.9 S 4.5 Cl 1.2 F 0.3 (LPSC‐AF). Hard‐soft acid‐base theory (HSAB) guided local‐bonding reconstruction increases the basicity and hard‐base character of SE ligands, strengthens P‐S coordination and passivates reactive P‐centered sites. Consequently, the 1,2,5,6‐anthracenetetrone (ATO) adsorption energy decreases from −4.41 to −0.15 eV, suppressing interfacial acid‐base coordination, nucleophilic attack and coupled redox reactions. LPSC‐AF retains an ionic conductivity of 3.8 mS cm −1 and supports stable lithium plating/stripping for over 3000 h. ATO‐based ASSLMBs deliver 358.3 mAh g −1 with 100% initial Coulombic efficiency and retain 81% capacity after 2000 cycles at 5 C and 60°C. The approach is also applicable to C4Q cathodes, establishing HSAB‐guided SEs redesign as a route to stable all‐solid‐state lithium‐organic batteries.

item.title: Hard‐Acid High‐Entropy Stabilized Chloride Octahedra for Halide Solid Electrolytes at High‐Voltage of 4.8 V
item.description: ABSTRACT Halide solid‐state electrolytes (HSSEs) are promising candidates for high‐energy‐density all‐solid‐state lithium batteries (ASSLBs). However, the instability of the metal‐chloride (M‐Cl) octahedra remains a major obstacle to their operation under ultrahigh‐voltage conditions. In chloride electrolytes such as Li 3 InCl 6 , the elongated weak M‐Cl bond can trigger structural degradation and induce Cl − oxidation during the charging process. Herein, guided by the strong hard acid‐hard base interaction between metal cations and Cl − (hard base), a hard‐acid high‐entropy halide electrolyte, Li 2.5 In 0.5 Y 0.1 Al 0.1 Zr 0.1 Ta 0.2 Cl 6 , is developed through the synergistic incorporation of multiple hard‐acid cations. Structural and electronic analyses reveal that the hard‐acid high‐entropy strategy can stabilize M‐Cl octahedra and chloride electronic states, thereby suppressing chloride oxidation and enhancing stability at 4.8 V. Meanwhile, the modified framework creates a more favorable Li + migration pathway, enabling a high ionic conductivity of 2.38 mS cm −1 . When paired with an ultrahigh‐nickel NCM955 cathode, the resulting ASSLB exhibits outstanding electrochemical performance, retaining over 80% of its capacity after 1400 cycles at 10 C and 4.8 V while maintaining stable operation at ‐20°C. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of hard‐acid high‐entropy engineering in simultaneously enhancing oxidative stability and Li + transport, providing a new crystal‐chemistry design strategy for ultrahigh‐voltage halide solid electrolytes.

item.title: Radical Bearing Solid Electrolyte Interface as an Active Ionic Reservoir for Fast Li+ Storage in Coordination Confined Fe@C Anodes
item.description: ABSTRACT High capacity anodes rely on diffusion limited bulk reactions that induce structural strain, compromising fast and durable Li + storage. Here, carbon‐coated Fe nanocomposites (Fe@C) are constructed through a MOF‐derived coordination confinement strategy that suppresses Fe nanoparticle coalescence and preserves Fe‐centered interfaces for space charge storage, with a protective carbon shell contributing some capacity. This interfacial pathway minimizes strain and shortens charge transport distances, enabling a reversible capacity of 565 mAh g −1 at 2C. With electron accumulation in metal 3d states recognized as the electronic component of space charge storage, the remaining question is how the compensating Li + is accommodated within the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). In situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy tracks the reversible formation of the SEI, and ex situ analyses identify organic polymers as the main components for Li + storage. In situ electron paramagnetic resonance with spin trapping captures reversible carbon‐chain radical evolution associated with Li + accommodation. Together, these findings reveal a radical bearing polymeric SEI that undergoes Fe‐catalyzed dynamic reconstruction and serves as the ionic component of space charge storage. This work links coordination confined interface design with radical mediated SEI chemistry, establishing an active ionic reservoir for fast interfacial Li + storage.

item.title: Enhancing Interfacial Stability Between NASICON‐Type Solid‐State Electrolyte and Lithium Metal Anode via Multifunctional Synergistic Interface Engineering
item.description: ABSTRACT Li 1.3 Al 0.3 Ti 1.7 (PO 4 ) 3 (LATP)‐based all‐solid‐state lithium metal batteries (ASSLMBs) hold exceptional promise for achieving high energy density and excellent safety, yet their practical application is severely hindered by critical interfacial issues, including poor contact, side reactions, and dendrite growth. Herein, a flexible multifunctional composite interlayer (PVGa) composed of Poly(vinylidene fluoride‐co‐hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF‐HFP), Lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), and gallium(III) fluoride (GaF 3 ) is constructed at the LATP/Li interface via a facile solution drop‐casting method. The polymer matrix effectively fills interfacial voids, homogenizes current distribution, and suppresses side reactions, while GaF 3 undergoes in situ alloying with the Li anode to form a uniform and dense LiF/Li x Ga hybrid SEI layer with high ionic conductivity and interfacial energy, guiding homogeneous Li deposition. Benefiting from this synergistic effect, the LATP@PVGa symmetric cell achieves a critical current density of 1.9 mA cm −2 and exhibits stable cycling over 6000 h at 0.1 mA cm −2 and 4500 h at 0.2 mA cm −2 . Moreover, LiFePO 4 full cells retain 86.7% capacity after 1100 cycles at 0.5 C, demonstrating excellent practical application potential. This work provides a novel and effective strategy to address the multifaceted interfacial challenges in LATP‐based ASSLMBs.

item.title: Homogenizing Stress Distribution to Construct a Stable LiF‐rich Solid Electrolyte Interphase in Silicon/Carbon Anodes
item.description: ABSTRACT Inducing homogeneous stress distribution is essential for enhancing the structural stability of silicon/carbon (Si/C) anodes. To this end, a liquid‐phase synthesis approach combined with an electrochemical technique is proposed to in situ construct a robust LiF‐rich interphase on the Si/C surface. Both the functional interphase and pre‐designed void within the carbon layer induce a stable LiF‐rich solid electrolyte interface (SEI) through their synergistic management of anisotropic stress evolution, significantly increasing interfacial mechanical strength, suppressing electrode polarization and electron leakage into the electrolyte, and achieving superior interface stability. Fatigue resistance, theoretical simulations, and electrode surface analyses reveal that stress concentration and catastrophic strain localization are effectively restrained, causing an intact interface and reduced energy barriers for Li + de‐solvation and diffusion. The dQ/dV curves and voltage drop analysis disclose a more reversible phase transition process for Li 15 Si 4 in the optimal electrode upon cycling. These factors are collectively attributed to the homogeneous stress distribution. Therefore, the optimized electrode delivers outstanding electrochemical robustness, achieving 96.5% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 4 A g −1 and a rate capacity of 589.5 mAh g −1 at 6 A g −1 . The proposed strategy, homogenizing stress distribution, offers a novel paradigm for constructing a stable SEI on electrodes undergoing severe volume fluctuations.

item.title: Cyclic Nonequilibrium Processing of Halide Solid Electrolytes for Low‐Pressure Operation of all‐Solid‐State Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Sluggish ionic transport and high rigidity of inorganic solid electrolytes (SSEs) necessitate ultra‐high external pressures in all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs), posing a major barrier to their deployment. Herein, we propose a cyclic nonequilibrium thermal process for Li 3 InCl 6 (LIC) solid electrolyte, which is implemented through repeated quenching to concurrently optimize ionic transport and deformability. The initial quench refines particle size, whereas subsequent quenching induces local amorphization, thereby suppressing grain boundary resistance and enhancing compressibility. Meanwhile, additional Li vacancies are introduced, accelerating bulk phase ionic transport. These coupled mesoscopic and microscopic structural evolutions increase the room‐temperature ionic conductivity (IC) of LIC from 1.3 to 6.8 mS/cm, while reducing the Young's modulus from 42.3 to 17.6 GPa. The optimized LIC enables a stable cycling of ASSBs at a low operation pressure of 2 MPa with a high areal capacity of 7.7 mAh/cm 2 , highlighting cyclic nonequilibrium processing as a promising route for practical ASSBs.

item.title: Suppressing Mg2+‐Induced Failure of LATP Membranes for Lithium Separation Using a Low‐Barrier Graphite Interface
item.description: ABSTRACT High Mg/Li ratios and coexisting ions in salt‐lake brines limit the long‐term selectivity and structural stability of Li 1.3 Al 0.3 Ti 1.7 (PO 4 ) 3 (LATP) membranes. To address interfacial mass‐transfer resistance and Mg 2+ ‐induced performance decay, a graphite‐PVDF‐coated LATP membrane is constructed, enabling low‐resistance Li + transport while mitigating Mg 2+ interference. Under optimized conditions, the membrane increases Li + flux by ∼27% relative to pristine LATP, achieving a maximum Li–Mg separation factor of ∼6200 and a decreased water contact angle, indicating improved migration of hydrated Li + . Calculations show a lower Li + migration barrier in graphite than in LATP (0.27 vs. 0.68 eV), providing a low‐resistance pathway. Graphite also adsorbs Mg‐solvated clusters more strongly than Li‐solvated ones, reducing local Mg 2+ enrichment at the interface. DFT calculations suggest that Mg 2+ substitutes Ti/Al sites, lowering the Li + /H + exchange energy by 62.34 meV and reducing the Li/Mg migration‐barrier difference from 1.19 to 0.45 eV. HRTEM/SAED shows that the graphite‐PVDF layer mitigates lattice disorder, and TEM‐EDS reveals lower local Mg in the coated LATP after operation (0.23 vs. 0.49 wt.%). Long‐term tests show a ∼5‐fold longer service lifetime than the pristine membrane, providing insights into interfacial design for durable LATP‐based electrodialysis.

item.title: High-resolution quantitative mapping of elastic heterogeneity in solid-state electrolytes via non-contact zero-group-velocity laser ultrasonics
item.description: Accurate quantification of the elastic properties of solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) and their spatial distributions is critical for understanding the electro-chemo-mechanical behaviors, such as dendrite growth and interfacial degradation, to ensure the long-term safety of next-generation solid-state batteries (SSBs). Existing methods, including ultrasonic velocity testing and nanoindentation, are typically limited to volume-averaged or surface-limited measurements, require physical contact, and often rely on prior material assumptions (e.g., Poisson’s ratio). These constraints hinder their ability to resolve intrinsic spatial heterogeneity in elastic properties. Here, a fully non-contact and non-destructive laser ultrasonic (LU) approach is developed for spatially resolved mapping of local elastic properties in SSEs. By exploiting localized zero-group-velocity (ZGV) resonances and thickness resonances (TR), the method enables simultaneous and high-resolution determination of Poisson’s ratio and elastic modulus without prior assumptions. The approach is demonstrated on Ta-doped LLZO and validated against contact ultrasonics and nanoindentation combined with scanning acoustic microscopy, showing strong agreement. Spatial LU mapping reveals elastic heterogeneity with a variation of ~4%, providing insight into potential microstructural inhomogeneity, stress localization, and non-uniform deposition. This work establishes LU as a powerful technique for non-invasive, high-resolution elastic characterization of SSEs, and provides a promising pathway toward in-line quality control for SSB manufacturing.

item.title: From Physics‐Informed Deep Learning to Experimental Realization: Unlocking Entropy‐Stabilized Titanium Halide Solid Electrolytes
item.description: ABSTRACT Accelerating the discovery of high‐performance solid electrolytes (SEs) is hindered by scarce experimental data and vast inorganic chemical spaces. Here, we present a physics‐informed deep learning platform that integrates a physics‐informed neural network with a dual‐source graph neural network. By embedding fundamental physical constraints (e.g., lattice stability and coulombic interactions) into the training process, our framework overcomes the small‐data dilemma, enabling the reliable screening of over 2 80 000 inorganic crystals. Guided by a multi‐objective optimization incorporating ionic conductivity, thermodynamic stability, and global economic factors, the titanium‐based halide family is identified as a cost‐effective alternative to scarce zirconium‐ or scandium‐based SEs. As a proof‐of‐concept, a novel Li 4 TiBr 4 Cl 4 electrolyte is synthesized, which exhibits a high room‐temperature ionic conductivity of 1.14 mS/cm. While 0 K density functional theory calculations predict an ordered layered ground state , structural characterization reveals a disordered cubic phase stabilized by configurational entropy at synthetic temperatures. Furthermore, all‐solid‐state lithium batteries incorporating this electrolyte deliver a stable long‐term cycling performance with a 90.6% capacity retention over 200 cycles at 0.5 C. This work demonstrates a closed‐loop discovery paradigm where physics‐constrained learning and thermodynamic understanding converge to realize high‐performance, economically viable energy materials.

item.title: Moisture‐ and Dendrite‐Resistant Argyrodite Electrolytes Enabled by Lithium‐ and Halogen‐Site Synergistic Substitutions for All‐Solid‐State Lithium Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Argyrodite electrolytes are promising for all‐solid‐state lithium batteries, while the high humid sensitivity and unstable interfacial reactions with lithium metal severely hinder practical application. In this work, a series of Li 5.4‐ x Ag x PS 4.4 Cl 1.6‐ x Br x ( x = 0, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, and 0.1) solid electrolytes with simultaneously enhanced ionic conductivity, air stability and lithium metal interfacial compatibility are synthesized via Ag and Br dual‐doping. Among them, Li 5.375 Ag 0.025 PS 4.4 Cl 1.575 Br 0.025 exhibits an increased room‐temperature ionic conductivity of 11.44 mS cm −1 after powder cold‐pressing, surpassing 10.22 mS cm −1 for the pristine Li 5.4 PS 4.4 Cl 1.6 . In addition, due to strong Ag‐S interactions, Li 5.375 Ag 0.025 PS 4.4 Cl 1.575 Br 0.025 releases only 0.752 cm 3 g −1 of H 2 S after air exposure, which is approximately only one third of that generated by the pristine Li 5.4 PS 4.4 Cl 1.6 . Benefiting from the in situ formation of a Li‐Ag alloy at the anode, Li 5.375 Ag 0.025 PS 4.4 Cl 1.575 Br 0.025 exhibits excellent lithium metal compatibility, enabling a critical current density of 1.55 mA cm −2 and stable lithium plating/stripping for 5000 h. Furthermore, the LiCoO 2 |Li 5.375 Ag 0.025 PS 4.4 Cl 1.575 Br 0.025 |Li cell demonstrates significantly improved cycling stability at a rate of 1 C, delivering a capacity retention of 84.5% after 1000 cycles. This work provides an effective strategy to simultaneously improve the chemical/electrochemical stability of argyrodite electrolytes, paving the way for the development of practical all‐solid‐state lithium batteries.

item.title: Polypyrrole as Dissociation Promoter and Interface Stabilizer of Solid Polymer Electrolytes for Solid‐State Li Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Advanced solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs) are indispensable for enabling durable, safe, and high‐energy‐density solid‐state lithium metal batteries (SSLMBs). However, the concurrent optimization of lithium‐salt dissociation, Li + transport, and lithium‐metal interfacial chemistry remains a challenge over decades. In this study, a PPy‐regulated solid polymer electrolyte (PPyPL) featuring chemically differentiated coordination sites is developed to reconstruct ion‐solvation chemistry through site‐selective Li + /anion coordination. The resulting coordination architecture affords differentiated molecular interactions in which pyrrolic nitrogen sites preferentially coordinate Li + , whereas hydrogen sites along the PPy backbone interact with bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI − ) anions, thereby simultaneously promoting lithium‐salt dissociation, accelerating Li + transport, and directing LiF/Li 3 N‐rich interphase formation. Benefiting from the synergistic regulation of ion‐solvation chemistry and interfacial evolution, PPyPL achieves an ionic conductivity of 0.76 mS cm −1 at room temperature (25°C), a Li + transference number of 0.65, and ultralong Li plating/stripping stability over 8000 h. It further enables outstanding rate capability and durable cycling in both Li||LiFePO 4 (LFP) and Li||LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 (NCM811) solid‐state full cells. This work provides a new strategy for regulating Li + /anion coordination in advanced SPEs toward durable SSLMBs.

item.title: Breaking Bottlenecks in Solid Electrolyte Discovery With Large Artificial Intelligence Models
item.description: ABSTRACT Solid electrolytes (SEs) are central to next‐generation metal batteries, yet their discovery remains constrained by fragmented data, limited transferability of simulations, and slow experimental iteration. Unlike catalysis, where surface reactivity dominates, SEs require simultaneous optimization of bulk ion transport, defect chemistry, mechanical integrity, and interfacial stability. Here, we outline a framework for autonomous SE discovery enabled by large artificial intelligence (AI) models, including machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and large language models (LLMs). We discuss the evolution from static materials databases to dynamic, self‐updating knowledge systems, the role of MLIPs in bridging density functional theory (DFT) and long‐timescale ion migration, and the emergence of LLMs as engines for literature mining, hypothesis generation, and scientific reasoning. We further describe a closed‐loop architecture integrating AI‐driven candidate design, multiscale simulation, uncertainty‐aware selection, and experimental validation. Such systems shift SE research from intuition‐guided exploration to data‐informed, self‐improving cycles. We conclude by highlighting challenges in data standardization, interfacial complexity, and reproducibility, and we propose design principles for building autonomous laboratories for solid‐state battery materials.

item.title: Minimal Transport Units Govern Oxygen‐Defect Stabilization and Transport for Lightweight Solid Electrolytes
item.description: ABSTRACT Solid electrolytes are central to electrochemical energy technologies, including fuel cells, sensors, catalysis, membrane separation, and electrolyser. However, most established oxide‐ion solid electrolytes are built around heavy B‐site cations embedded in rigid and highly connected coordination frameworks, leading to widespread high‐weight and sluggish ionic transport that is strongly coupled to large‐amplitude lattice relaxations. This intrinsic challenge hinders further performance optimization and constrains the rational design of lightweight electrolytes. Herein, we propose a minimal transport unit‐based design paradigm that combines simplified structural motifs with light‐element chemistry, enabled by the exceptional flexibility of B‐O polyhedra in coordination, rotation, deformation, and connectivity. As a proof of concept, Sc 1‐ x Zn x BO 3‐ x /2 , constructed from isolated BO 3 units, exhibits high oxide ion conductivity (σ(1000°C) ∼ 1.5 × 10 −2 S/cm), alongside excellent thermo‐mechanical stability. Oxygen vacancies are stabilized through the formation of B 2 O 5 units rather than isolated BO 2 species. Long‐range oxide‐ion migration is mediated by dynamic oxygen exchange between minimal BO 3 and B 2 O 5 units via continuous breaking and reforming of B 2 O 5 units, with transient BO 2 configurations as intermediates. This study demonstrates minimal transport units as a governing principle for defect stabilization and ionic conduction in lightweight solid electrolytes, offering a general design framework for portable and scalable high‐temperature energy technologies.

item.title: Reconfiguring Interfacial Electrochemical Potential for Boosting Sodium‐Ion Transport in Composite Solid Electrolytes
item.description: ABSTRACT Sluggish ion transport kinetics between the ceramic and polymer phases remain a key challenge in composite solid electrolytes (CSEs), primarily due to a severe interfacial barrier arising from their intrinsic physicochemical incompatibility. Herein, molecular design‐enabled electronic structure engineering is proposed to reconfigure the interfacial electrochemical environment at the Na 3 Zr 2 Si 2 PO 12 –poly(ethylene oxide) interface, based on a dual‐axis screening guided by the electron‐donating capability and molecular electronic asymmetry. By grafting different functional trimethoxysilanes from a targeted library onto the ceramic surface, the effect of the interfacial electrochemical potential on Na‐ion transport is investigated, revealing a strong negative correlation with the ionic conductivity of CSEs. The CSE with the optimal grafting molecule (phenyltrimethoxysilane) reduces the potential mismatch by 87% and lowers the Na‐ion migration barrier, thereby boosting Na‐ion conductivity by two orders of magnitude. All‐solid‐state sodium‐metal batteries using this CSE show boosted electrochemical performance with a high capacity of 91.8 mAh g −1 delivered at 5 C and retain ∼99% of their initial capacity after 500 cycles at 2 C. This work establishes a screening framework for reducing interfacial potential mismatch and addressing the long‐standing ion‐transport bottleneck across ceramic–polymer interfaces in CSEs.

item.title: Site‐Selective Anion‐Cation Regulation of Sulfide Electrolyte Enables Low‐Pressure Dendrite‐Suppressed All‐Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Achieving stable sulfide‐based all‐solid‐state lithium batteries with Li metal anodes and high‐capacity cathodes under low stack pressure is highly desirable for high‐energy‐density energy storage, but remains challenging because of unstable solid‐solid interfaces and dendrite‐induced short circuits. Here, we develop a site‐selective anion‐cation regulation strategy for argyrodite Li 6 PS 5 Cl electrolyte to couple framework stabilization with interphase chemistry, enabling long‐term dendrite‐suppressed cycling under low stack pressure. Al 3+ substitution for P 5+ forms AlS 4 ‐related local units and strengthens local Al–S bonding, stabilizing the sulfide framework against redox decomposition. Cl − incorporation into the 4 a /4 d anion sublattice promotes Li + transport, delivering a high room‐temperature ionic conductivity of 7.22 mS cm −1 . More importantly, F/Cl regulation redirects the interfacial decomposition pathway from a Li 2 S‐rich/LiCl interphase toward a LiF/LiCl‐rich and Li 2 S‐poor passivation layer, with exposed LiF/LiCl (200) planes that exhibit stronger interfacial adhesion with Li metal. Benefiting from this coupled framework‐interphase regulation, Li | LAPSCF‐Cl | Li symmetric cells cycle for over 8000 h at 0.5 mA cm −2 at 3 MPa and support stable cycling of both NCM811 and sulfur cathodes paired with Li metal under a relatively low pressure of 30 MPa.

item.title: Interfacial Instability of Halide Solid Electrolytes and Oxide Cathodes Under Low‐Humidity Dry‐Room Conditions
item.description: ABSTRACT Halide solid electrolytes are widely regarded as promising catholytes for all‐solid‐state batteries because of their high ionic conductivity, good deformability, and relative compatibility with oxide cathodes. However, their interfacial stability has been largely evaluated under inert laboratory conditions, whereas practical battery manufacturing is typically conducted in low‐humidity dry rooms rather than inert‐atmosphere gloveboxes. Here, we demonstrate that halide solid electrolyte/oxide cathode composite electrodes can undergo severe interfacial degradation even under a low‐humidity dry‐room environment with a dew point of −40°C. Using Li 3 InCl 6 and LiNi 0.83 Co 0.12 Mn 0.05 O 2 as a representative model system, we reveal that dry‐room exposure induces interfacial reactions that generate a passivation layer associated with hindered Li + transport, leading to markedly deteriorated electrochemical performance. Similar degradation behavior was also observed in several representative halide electrolyte/layered oxide combinations, suggesting that this issue is not limited to a single material pair. These findings identify a previously underappreciated processing‐induced interfacial challenge in halide‐based all‐solid‐state batteries and underscore the need to place greater emphasis on composite‐cathode stability under realistic dry‐room manufacturing conditions.

item.title: A PVDF‐Based Composite Solid Electrolyte Enabled by Carbon‐Free LiFePO4 for Stable Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Developing polymer‐based solid electrolytes with efficient Li + transport, electronic insulation, mechanical robustness, and stable electrode interfaces remains challenging for solid‐state lithium‐metal batteries. Here, a carbon‐free LiFePO 4 (LFP)/PVDF composite solid electrolyte is designed, where the intrinsically low electronic conductivity of LFP is transformed from a limitation for cathode applications into an electrolyte advantage. Unlike carbon‐coated LFP, carbon‐free LFP acts as an electronically insulating inorganic filler in the PVDF matrix, suppressing electron transport while promoting Li + migration through abundant LFP/PVDF interfaces. Optimized LFP50 exhibits an ionic conductivity of 4.89 × 10 −4 S cm −1 at 25°C, a Li + transport activation energy of 0.053 eV, an electronic conductivity on the order of 10 −10 S cm −1 , a 5.0 V oxidative stability window, and favorable mechanical properties. These features enable stable Li‐metal interfaces, as demonstrated by a critical current density of 6.2 mA cm −2 and uniform Li deposition. Furthermore, LFP50 provides lithium compensation through partial delithiation of cathode‐facing LFP particles, mitigating irreversible lithium loss. Without external pressure, Li|LFP50|LFP and Li|LFP50|NCM811 cells retain 93.8% and 80% capacity after 500 and 165 cycles, respectively. This work demonstrates carbon‐free LFP as a multifunctional filler strategy for regulating Li + transport, stabilizing electrode interfaces, and advancing solid‐state lithium‐metal batteries.

item.title: Anion‐Dipole Catalytic Decomposition Enables Robust Solid Electrolyte Interfaces for Ah‐Level Aqueous Zinc Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Constructing robust inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interfaces (SEIs) without the compromised safety and interfacial kinetics remains challenging for aqueous zinc ion batteries. Herein, we identify anion‐dipole binding energy and electrostatic potential difference as double descriptors for screening trace additives as molecular captors for anions, and propose an anion‐dipole catalytic decomposition strategy to tailor the SEI. Specifically, electron‐deficient aromatic acetophenone preferentially enters the electrical double layer, selectively recognizing and concentrating anions. Concurrently, it catalyzes anion decomposition by accelerating bond‐cleavage kinetics and reducing activation free energy, forming the inorganic‐rich SEI. This tailored interface yields a high Zn 2+ transference number (0.75), accelerates desolvation, and promotes planar (002)‐textured Zn deposition. Consequently, Zn//Zn symmetric cells exhibit exceptional cycling stability (7200 h), and an Ah‐level Zn//VO 2 pouch cell with cathode mass loading of 20 mg·cm −2 delivers a capacity of 4.28 Ah at 0.2 A·g −1 and retains 88.9% of its initial capacity after 100 cycles at 1 A·g −1 .

item.title: Local Symmetry Engineering Unlocks Stable Multi‐Electron Chemistry in NASICON Cathodes for High‐Energy‐Density Sodium‐Ion Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) hold great promise for large‐scale energy storage, but their advancement is constrained by the instability of multi‐electron redox reactions in cathode materials. In NASICON‐type phosphates, the high‐voltage V 4+ /V 5+ redox couple often suffers from poor reversibility, fundamentally rooted in the trade‐off between redox activity and structural stability. Here, we demonstrate that this limitation can be overcome by a local symmetry engineering strategy that precisely regulates the [VO 6 ] octahedra. Leveraging the complementary ionic radii and electronic configurations of Fe 2+ and Al 3+ , the co‐substitution achieves a controlled symmetry reduction of the [VO 6 ] units while maintaining the structural integrity of the NASICON framework. This symmetry reduction triggers a reconfiguration of the V 3d orbitals and promotes electron delocalization. Experimental and theoretical analyses confirm the electrochemical performance strongly depends on the symmetry of [VO 6 ] octahedra: moderate symmetry reduction enhances cycling stability, whereas excessive reduction leads to performance degradation. The optimized Na 3.6 V 1.2 Fe 0.6 Al 0.2 (PO 4 ) 3 cathode exhibits a high reversible capacity of 151.4 mAh g −1 corresponding to a 2.6‐electron transfer and exceptional cycling stability (84.6% capacity retention after 10,000 cycles at 20C). This work establishes octahedral symmetry engineering as an effective strategy to unlock stable multi‐electron redox chemistry in polyanionic cathodes.

item.description: Thin sulfide electrolyte membranes are prone to fracture, poor interparticle contact, and interrupted Li⁺ transport during processing. Herein, we report a pre-fibrillated polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)-assisted solvent-free dry-processing strategy for flexible Li₆PS₅Cl (LPSCl) membranes. Preformed PTFE fibers were blended with LPSCl powder and converted into dense membranes by roll pressing. The optimized membrane containing 0.5 wt% PTFE was approximately 60 μm thick, free-standing, and foldable, while delivering an ionic conductivity of 2.03 mS cm⁻¹, an apparent activation energy of 28.42 kJ mol⁻¹, and an electronic conductivity of 5.33 × 10⁻¹² S cm⁻¹ at 25 °C. A Li–In/LPSCl–PTFE/Li–In symmetric cell maintained stable polarization for 200 h at 0.1 mA cm⁻² under a constant stack pressure of 30 MPa. A LiNbO₃-coated NCM811/LPSCl–PTFE/Li–In full cell delivered an initial discharge capacity of 188.88 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.1 C and retained 155.51 mAh g⁻¹ after 200 cycles at 25 °C, with Coulombic efficiencies above 97% after the first cycle. item.title: Tailored Stereo‐Configuration of Crosslinkable Polyester‐Based Solid Polymer Electrolytes for All‐Solid‐State and Binder‐Free Li Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT By harnessing stereoisomerism in unsaturated polyesters, we elucidate how subtle structural variations impact Li + solvation structures by modulating free volume, Li + diffusivity, and lithium salt dissociation within solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs). The intrinsic reactivity of C═C bonds along the polymeric backbones is further exploited via a facile UV‐curing approach to construct robust three‐dimensional polymeric networks that impart mechanical robustness and preferential restriction of TFSI − mobility relative to Li + transport. The distorted conformation of poly( n ‐pentyl maleate) (PPM) leads to sparsely crosslinked structures, preserving efficient Li + transport pathways. Furthermore, end‐group fluorination enhances interfacial stability by facilitating the formation of a LiF‐rich solid electrolyte interphase. These synergistic design strategies culminate in a crosslinked PPM‐based SPE (XL‐PPM‐3F‐Li) featuring one CF 3 end‐capping group, which exhibits remarkable electrochemical durability in both Li||Li symmetric and LFP full‐cell configurations. Furthermore, this advantage is extended to the device level by integrating binder, electrolyte, and separator into a single ultrathin (∼“5 µm‐thick”) crosslinked SPE that conformally interfaces with the electrode microstructure. This integrated configuration markedly lowers interfacial and charge‐transfer resistance, enabling 65% of the initial reversible capacity at 2 C and 93.6% retention after 100 cycles at 0.5 C (60°C). Overall, this crosslinking‐enabled unified architecture establishes a robust strategy for ultra‐stable solid‐state lithium‐metal batteries.

item.title: Multi‐Li+ Coordination for Superior Room‐Temperature Ionic Conductivity in PEO Solid Electrolytes
item.description: ABSTRACT Ion transport in poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) electrolytes is severely constrained by sluggish Li + mobility arising from tight chelation of ether oxygens, and by insufficient lithium salt dissociation. Inspired by polycarboxylate ether (PCE) superplasticizers in cement, we demonstrate phosphonate‐functionalized PCE (P‐PCE) could overcome both limitations. The electron‐rich ‐PO 3 2– groups could liberate Li + from the strong Li + ‐PEO chelation and promote efficient salt dissociation without trapping Li + . Instead, they facilitate rapid Li + migration through a unique multi‐Li + coordination mechanism, where the electrostatic repulsion among multiple Li + ions coordinated to a single ‐PO 3 2– destabilizes solvation and promotes rapid Li + hopping between adjacent sites. Meanwhile, P‐PCE suppresses PEO crystallization and, through multi‐Li + coordination, induces a more extended conformation of PEO, which fosters high‐entropy Li + coordination environments involving TFSI – , ether oxygens, and ‐PO 3 2– in transient combinations, promoting long‐range Li + transport. The simultaneously enhanced Li + concentration and mobility lead to a high ionic conductivity (1.7 × 10 −4 S cm −1 , 30°C) without adding liquid plasticizers. Correspondingly, Li||LiFePO 4 cells deliver high capacities of 140.6 mAh g −1 at 0.5 C and 119.7 mAh g −1 at 1 C (30°C). This work provides a simple yet effective strategy for developing high‐performance solid‐state batteries and molecular‐level insights for rational polymer electrolyte designs.

item.title: Role of Structural Disorder on Phonon Transport and Thermal Conductivity in Li6PS5Br
item.description: ABSTRACT Sulfidic solid electrolytes pose a promising material class for enabling solid‐state batteries. While their defect chemistry and ion transport have been studied extensively, thermal transport and its interplay with ion dynamics remain poorly understood, despite the exceptionally low thermal conductivities of these materials. Here, we investigate the relationship between structural disorder, ion dynamics, and thermal properties in the argyrodite Li 6 PS 5 Br using neural network potential molecular dynamics, mesoscale modeling, and experimental techniques. By systematically varying Br − /S 2− site inversion, we demonstrate its strong influence on lattice dynamics and Li + diffusion. Increasing anion disorder broadens the vibrational density of states and promotes liquid‐like Li + dynamics resulting in significantly enhanced ionic transport. In contrast, thermal transport remains largely unaffected by the degree of site inversion. Both anion‐ordered and anion‐disordered Li 6 PS 5 Br exhibit similarly low bulk thermal conductivities of approximately 0.4 W·m −1 ·K −1 with only weak temperature dependence between 100 and 900 K. Experimental and computational analyses of the transport mechanisms reveal that thermal transport in this temperature range is primarily governed by diffuson‐like modes. Excellent agreement between experimental and computational results is achieved by bridging molecular dynamics simulations with mesoscale modeling to incorporate porosity effects.

item.title: Porous Solid Electrolyte Reactors for Function‐Oriented Off‐Electrode Electrosynthesis
item.description: ABSTRACT Electrosynthesis offers an attractive route to sustainable chemical manufacturing when coupled with renewable electricity. As electrosynthesis capability advances towards high‐purity products, the traditional proximity of reaction products to the electrode surface, where the reaction happens, increasingly becomes a limiting factor. In addition, the formation and transport of reactive species are confined in the same chamber, resulting in electrolyte contamination of the product. Porous solid electrolyte (PSE) reactors address this spatial constraint by introducing an additional ion‐conductive middle layer between the cathode and anode, enabling a versatile off‐electrode space for product formation and transportation. Here, we frame PSE reactors as function‐oriented platforms for off‐electrode electrosynthesis, in which the PSE middle layer serves as a functional reaction space that enables ionic recombination, reaction‐environment regulation, and improved management of reactive intermediates. By linking the underlying ionic‐species transport mechanisms and reactor design principles, we establish a structure‐transport‐function framework for understanding how PSE reactors extend electrosynthesis beyond the electrode surface confinement and guide the rational design of scalable electrosynthesis reactors as on‐site chemical manufacturing platforms.

item.title: Potassium Regulation at Na1 Sites for Enhanced Redox Utilization and Structural Reversibility in Multimetal NASICON Cathodes
item.description: ABSTRACT NASICON polyanionic cathodes are widely studied because they combine structural stability, low cost, and superior rate capability for sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). However, local lattice strain and sluggish multielectron redox kinetics during deep (de)sodiation limit the energy density and lifespan of NASICON cathodes. Here, we regulate Na1 sites with potassium in the multimetal NASICON cathode Na 3 K 0.6 V 1.4 Mn 0.3 Fe 0.3 (PO 4 ) 3 (NKVMFP). Calculations and experiments indicate that K occupation at Na1 sites regulates the alkali ion environment, which in turn modifies the MnO 6 crystal field, improves Mn/V redox utilization, and suppresses Na + /vacancy ordering. NKVMFP delivers an energy density of 381 Wh kg −1 , sustains 12,000 cycles at 4 A g −1 , and shows a volume variation of 4.13%; its stable operation in a 320 mAh pouch cell further supports its practical potential. These results show that Na1 site alkali ion regulation can improve redox utilization and structural reversibility in multimetal NASICON cathodes.

item.title: Grape Cluster Inspired Biomimetic Composite Solid Electrolyte for High‐Voltage and Long‐Life Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Solid‐state lithium metal batteries suffer from poor interfacial stability and dendrite growth, primarily limited by the ion transport kinetics and mechanical properties of composite solid electrolytes (CSE). Inspired by the hierarchical grape cluster, we design a biomimetic electrolyte via electrospinning PAN fiber “pedicel” integrated with mesoporous SiO 2 ‐SO 3 Li “grape berry” fillers, followed by in‐situ polymerization. This structure establishes long‐range Li + conduction channels and a robust physical barrier, delivering a high Li + transference number of 0.65, ionic conductivity of 1.44 × 10 −3 S cm −1 at 25°C, and a modulus of 520 MPa. Benefiting from these advantages, the assembled LFP|Li and NCM811|Li cells achieve 88.8% capacity retention after 1000 cycles and 94.3% after 300 cycles, respectively. Moreover, a high‐loading pouch cell realizes an energy density of 414.9 Wh kg −1 /797.8 Wh L −1 and withstands harsh abuse tests. Mechanistically, DFT and phase‐field simulations reveal the dual Li + pathways and TFSI − immobilization enabled by the ‐SO 3 Li groups. Notably, a physics‐informed neural network (PINN) framework decouples interface activation‐aging kinetics and predicts long‐term impedance evolution. This work provides a biomimetic paradigm and data‐driven methods for the design and interface analysis of high‐performance CSE.

item.title: Ultra‐High Ionic Conductivity Sulfide‐Based Composite Membranes Paired With Stable Interfacial Layer Enables High‐Energy‐Density All‐Solid‐State Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Intrinsic properties of sulfide solid‐state electrolytes (SEs) are crucial for achieving all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs) with high safety and high energy density, yet it is challenging to fabricate high‐performance sulfide SE films in a scalable approach. Furthermore, the inevitable side reactions between sulfide SE and lithium metal anodes exacerbate interfacial incompatibility, causing degradation in the cyclic stability. Here, a high‐performance sulfide SE (Li 5.4 PS 4.4 Cl 0.8 Br 0.8 ) was selected as the base phase to compensate for the loss of electrochemical performance during the dry film‐forming process. It was then combined with Polytetrafluoroethylene binder to prepare a high‐ionic‐conductivity composite membrane (HICCM). To mitigate side reactions between HICCM and the anode, a LiF‐rich interfacial layer forms in situ on the lithium metal surface, and the assembled symmetric cell achieves a high critical current density of 1.3 mA cm −2 and stable cycling for 2000 h (0.2 mA cm −2 ). For electrochemical performance, HICCM exhibits fast ion transport kinetics and electrical insulation, allowing the ASSB configured as FeS 2 //HICCM//LiF‐Li to achieve an energy density of 416.5 Wh kg −1 at a high loading of 3.4 mAh cm −2 . This work demonstrates that by combining HICCM with a stable interface design, ASSBs can achieve longevity and high cell‐level energy density.

item.title: Anion Engineering of Sulfide Solid Electrolytes: From Fundamentals to High‐Performance All‐Solid‐State Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Sulfide‐based solid‐state electrolytes (SSSEs) have emerged as one of the most promising materials for next‐generation all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs), owing to their high ionic conductivity, favorable mechanical properties, and compatibility with high‐energy‐density electrode materials. This review presents a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in the anion engineering of SSSEs, with a focus on the central role of the anionic sublattice in governing lithium‐ion transport. We discussed the structural families of sulfide electrolytes, elucidated the mechanisms of lithium‐ion conduction, and examined how anion disorder and polarizability influence conduction pathways and activation energies. The primary focus of this review was on strategies involving anion substitution and modification, including single‐ and multi‐element doping, multi‐anion frameworks, and heterostructure designs, and their effects on electrochemical stability, interfacial compatibility, and mechanical properties. We further reviewed the electrochemical performance metrics, scalability, and processing challenges associated with these materials. Finally, we outlined current limitations and future perspectives on a roadmap toward commercial implementation, highlighting the potential of anion‐engineered SSSEs to enable safe, high‐performance, and sustainable energy storage in next‐generation lithium‐ion batteries.

item.title: A Stress Dispersive Quasi‐Solid Polymer Electrolyte Enables Ah‐Level Impact Tolerant Lithium‐Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT To maintain reliable voltage output under dynamic impact conditions, intrinsic, materials‐level strategies are urgently needed to stabilize high‐energy Li batteries. Here, a stress dispersive quasi‐solid polymer electrolyte (SDPE) is proposed by constructing a crosslinked network from boroxine‐junction tris(aryl‐amide)‐linked poly(2,2′‐disulfonyl‐4,4′‐benzidine terephthalamide) for Ah‐level Li batteries. This electrolyte integrates an ultra‐rigid backbone for load distribution with more compliant boroxine junctions to accommodate localized deformation. As a result, it enables a durable Li plating/stripping for over 1400 h and delivers a high discharge capacity of 476.8 mAh g −1 in Li/Cr 8 O 21 primary batteries, while retaining 77.2% of the initial capacity after 7 days of storage at 60°C. Importantly, this intrinsic stability translates to device‐level reliability. Ah‐level pouch cells employing SDPE maintain a stable open‐circuit voltage under impacts exceeding 19,000 g, whereas the liquid‐electrolyte counterpart exhibits an immediate 384 mV voltage drop. Moreover, no hazardous response is observed even under nail penetration of the pouch cell. Combined with force‐constant analysis revealing a stiff‐skeleton/compliant‐junction stress‐transfer hierarchy, these results establish a direct structure–function linkage between molecular design and impact‐tolerant energy delivery. This work provides a viable pathway toward intrinsically resilient batteries for operation under extreme mechanical conditions.

item.title: Engineering a borate-rich interphase for highly stable all-solid-state sodium batteries
item.description: Composite polymer electrolytes (CPEs) are promising for all-solid-state sodium batteries, yet interfacial instability limits their practical applications. The commonly used NaTFSI can electrochemically form an NaF–Na2CO3–Na2O-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) to regulate sodium-ion deposition, but the resulting protective layer still suffers from early failure. Herein, a boron-enriched interphase is introduced by incorporating NaDFOB into a polyethylene-oxide based CPE, enabling stable and dendrite-free Na plating/stripping. Experimental results reveal that DFOB− preferentially decomposes over TFSI−, forming an Na4B2O5–NaF–Na2CO3–Na2O SEI with synergistic ion-conductive and electron-blocking properties. Moreover, theoretical calculations are performed to investigate the synergistic ionic-enhanced and electronic-restricted capability of the SEI layer. Benefiting from the stabilized SEI, the Na||Na symmetric cell exhibits outstanding cyclic stability (5,000 h at 0.5 mA cm−2) and full cell delivers a high initial capacity of 99.4 mAh g−1 with 92.38% retention at 3 C after 9,000 cycles.

item.title: Super‐Toughness Self‐Healing Composite Solid Electrolyte With Structured Interfacial Reconstruction Enabling Fast Ion Transport and Stable Interface for High‐Performance Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Lithium–metal batteries are widely regarded as a key direction for next‐generation energy storage systems due to high energy density. However, LiNi 0 . 8 Co 0 . 1 Mn 0 . 1 O 2 ||Li battery systems face severe challenges in practical application, including lithium dendrite growth, interfacial side reactions and structural degradation of high‐nickel cathodes. Here, we proposed a versatile modification strategy combining in‐situ interfacial transformation with polymer phase regulation to fabricate self‐healing solid polymer electrolyte with fast ion transport and stable interface. This strategy not only constructs fast ion channels and suppresses hydrofluoric acid production by in‐situ converting Li 2 CO 3 on the Li 6.4 La 3 Zr 1.4 Ta 0.6 O 12 surface into Li 2 PO 3 F interfacial layer, but also induces the transition of PVDF from α‐phase to high polarity β‐phase using ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid to promote lithium salt dissolution and reduce Li + migration resistance. The as‐prepared electrolyte exhibits extended electrochemical voltage windows (5.13 V), high room‐temperature ionic conductivity (1.694 mS cm − 1 ), excellent thermal stability (200°C), high elongation at break (422.6%), and superior cycling stability (89.4% retention after 500 cycles at 1 C). A non‐destructive monitoring method based on d p /|d Q | and d T /|d Q | differential signals has been developed to track electrochemical‐mechanical‐thermal responses during battery operation. This work provides an effective strategy for designing solid polymer electrolytes with high ionic conductivity and interfacial stability.

item.title: Quantifying the Dissolution of Organic and Inorganic Components in Solid Electrolyte Interphase for Sodium‐Ion Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Anode interphase dissolution is a major cause of instability in sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) because Na‐based solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) compounds are more soluble than their Li analogues. Here, glyme electrolytes with varied chain lengths are used to regulate Na + solvation structure and clarify its effect on SEI dissolution. A component‐resolved framework combining ion chromatography, mass spectrometry, electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance, and X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy is developed to quantify the dissolution and retention of organic and inorganic SEI species. This approach determines absolute SEI retention rather than relying on aggregate interphase loss. Compared with the glyme, tetraglyme reduces total SEI dissolution from 75% to 53% and increases the retention of inorganic F‐containing species from 18% to 30%. This improvement arises from an anion‐enriched Na + solvation shell, which promotes the formation of a thinner, denser, and more inorganic‐rich SEI. Consequently, 1.25 Ah NaNi 1/3 Fe 1/3 Mn 1/3 O 2 ||hard carbon pouch cells using the tetraglyme‐based electrolyte retain 91.2% capacity after 500 cycles and exhibit stable voltage retention during 21‐day aging at 60°C. These results establish a quantitative methodology for distinguishing the dissolution behavior of organic and inorganic SEI components, reveal the role of ether chain length in interphase stability, and provide practical guidance for designing durable SIBs.

item.title: Defect‐Free Transfer Principles for Scalable, Thin Garnet‐Based Hybrid Solid Electrolytes in Solid‐State Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT The scalable fabrication of thin, uniform, and defect‐free hybrid solid electrolytes (HSEs) remains a critical challenge for solid‐state batteries due to the lack of quantitative design principles governing interfacial interactions during coating, transfer, and impregnation. Here, we establish thermodynamic criteria for Li 6 . 75 La 3 Zr 1 . 75 Ta 0 . 25 O 12 ‐based hybrid layers (LLZTO‐HLs) fabrication using Hansen solubility parameters to correlate interfacial compatibility with process behavior. Uniform coating requires sufficiently high slurry–substrate compatibility, whereas clean transfer demands low binder–substrate adhesion. Furthermore, binder–polymer electrolyte compatibility governs impregnation behavior, enabling rational combination selection. Based on this framework, defect‐free, 15 µm‐thin LLZTO‐HLs are fabricated over large areas (120 cm 2 ) via transfer printing and integrated into transfer‐printed HSEs (THSEs). Compared with direct coating, transfer printing enables uniform electrolyte layers and electrode interfacial stability owing to the absence of slurry infiltration into the porous anode. Consequently, THSEs exhibit enhanced Li + transport, superior rate capability, and improved cycling stability in coin‐type hybrid solid‐state batteries. Notably, comparable cycling performance is retained in pouch‐type cells despite increased cell area, highlighting the excellent uniformity and scalability of the THSE. The THSE demonstrates superior thermal stability under elevated temperatures. The thermodynamic design principles established herein provide a generalizable framework for scalable manufacturing of high‐performance HSEs.

item.title: Redox Decoupling Modulates Multi‐Electron Reaction in Mn‐Rich NASICON Cathode for High‐Energy Sodium‐Ion Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Coupled redox reactions caused by voltage hysteresis limit the application of Mn‐rich NASICON cathodes for sodium‐ion batteries. Herein, this work fabricates a Na 3.6 Mn 1.25 Ti 0.7 Ni 0.05 (PO 4 ) 3 (NM1.25TP‐Ni) cathode material achieving redox decoupling of Mn/Ti. Specifically, the introduction of an appropriate amount of Ni effectively facilitates the redox reaction of Mn 2 + /Mn 3 + and significantly accelerates its reaction kinetics, thereby achieving effective separation of the electrochemical active regions of Mn and Ti. Crucially, the in situ electrochemical impedance spectra based on distribution relaxation time shows that the redox decoupling effect achieves kinetic decoupling of Mn/Ti by stabilizing the local coordination environment and specifically accelerating the charge transfer process of Mn 2+ /Mn 3+ . Furthermore, the enhanced kinetics effectively suppress voltage hysteresis in the high‐voltage region, ensuring the full occurrence of the Mn 3+ /Mn 4+ redox reaction. Consequently, NM1.25TP‐Ni exhibits an excellent capacity output (166.3 mAh g −1 ) and a high practical energy density (467.6 Wh kg −1 ). This work establishes that redox decoupling as an effective paradigm for overcoming the kinetic barriers in Mn‐rich NASICON cathodes with multi‐electron reactions provides a new approach for the design of high energy density materials for sodium‐ion batteries.

item.title: Ultra‐Stable Vanadium‐Based Zinc‐Ion Batteries via Complete Confinement of Free Water Into Bound Water by an Organic–Inorganic Viscoelastic Solid Electrolyte
item.description: ABSTRACT Vanadium‐based zinc‐ion batteries suffer from severe vanadium dissolution, cathode collapse, and an unstable zinc anode interface in free‐water dominated aqueous electrolytes, particularly under low current densities where long‐term cyclability remains unattainable. Here, we design a bound‐water dominated organic–inorganic viscoelastic solid electrolyte (VSE) to realize ultra‐stable vanadium‐based ZIBs. The VSE can completely convert free water into bound water through abundant hydrogen‐bonding sites from PEG4000 and SiO 2 components. Density functional theory calculations reveal that PEG4000 preferentially adsorbs on the NH 4 V 4 O 10 (NVO) surface with a binding energy of −0.942 eV, raising the vanadium vacancy formation energy to 0.838 eV and thus fundamentally suppressing vanadium dissolution. Meanwhile, this bound‐water dominated solidified electrolyte significantly stabilizes the zinc anode interface, suppressing the diffusion of soluble vanadium species, and the viscoelastic structure simultaneously provides high ionic conductivity (3.14 mS cm −1 ). Consequently, the Zn|VSE|Zn symmetric cell achieves an ultra‐long cycling life exceeding 8500 h, and the Zn|VSE|NVO full cell can stably cycle more than 8000 cycles at 1.0 A g −1 and maintain 93.2% capacity retention over 1084 cycles even at 0.2 A g −1 . This work establishes a “water confinement” electrolyte strategy to resolve cathode degradation and anode instability, offering a practical path toward durable ZIBs.

item.title: Dual‐Functional PDA/CMC‐Li Supramolecular Bridging Networks Unlock Trans‐Phase Li+ Conduction in Composite Solid Electrolytes for High‐Performance Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Composite solid electrolytes (CSEs) hold immense promise for high‐energy‐density solid‐state lithium metal batteries, yet their practical application remains severely hampered by filler agglomeration and sluggish interfacial Li + transport. Herein, dual‐functional supramolecular bridging networks are constructed by employing lithiated carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC‐Li) as dynamic bridges to interconnect polydopamine (PDA)‐modified Li 6.28 Al 0.24 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (LLZAO) fillers within a PVDF‐HFP matrix. This synergistic architecture helps promote a more uniform filler dispersion and actively mediates ion solvation dynamics via simultaneous anion trapping and cation extraction. Crucially, this dual‐regulation fundamentally mitigates the space‐charge layer (SCL) effect at organic‐inorganic boundaries, actively unlocking a highly efficient trans‐phase Li + percolation pathway through the LLZAO ceramic bulk, thereby bypassing conventionally sluggish interfacial routes. The resulting spatially homogeneous ion flux may reduce localized current hotspots and suppress lithium dendrite proliferation. Consequently, the optimized PVPL electrolyte empowers Li||Li symmetrical cells to maintain stable plating/stripping over 1400 h. Furthermore, LiFePO 4 ||PVPL||Li full cells deliver 83% capacity retention after 400 cycles at 2 C, while NCM811||PVPL||Li cells maintain 88% capacity retention over 200 cycles. This dual‐functional bridging strategy establishes a generalizable and effective paradigm for engineering advanced CSEs with optimized structural and Li + transport kinetics.

item.title: Building‐Block Design of Nonflammable Quasi‐Solid Electrolytes for Ampere‐Hour‐Scale Sodium‐Ion Batteries
item.description: ABSTRACT Sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) are emerging as a competitive technology for large‐scale energy storage; however, their commercial viability remains severely hindered by the inherent flammability and high volatility of liquid electrolytes (LEs). Herein, we propose a modular assembly strategy inspired by the building‐block principle to architect a quasi‐solid electrolyte (QSE). By synergistically integrating vinylene carbonate (VC) and 2,2,3,4,4,4‐hexafluorobutyl acrylate (HFBA) monomers, we modulate the electron density distribution within the polymer matrix. The resulting PVH QSE lowers the Na + desolvation barrier and provides continuous ion migration pathways, thereby achieving exceptional ionic conductivity of 5.60 mS cm −1 and a sodium‐ion transference number of 0.58. Furthermore, the spatially locked polymer architecture drives the formation of ion‐solvent aggregates and a robust NaF‐rich solid electrolyte interphase, synergistically suppressing solvent decomposition and eradicating sodium dendrite growth. Consequently, the Na||Na 3 V 2 (PO 4 ) 3 cells exhibit an outstanding capacity retention of 94.9% after 3000 cycles alongside superior temperature adaptability. To demonstrate practical feasibility, the hard carbon||NaNi 0.33 Fe 0.33 Mn 0.33 O 2 pouch cells maintain stable cycling over 200 cycles. Crucially, nail penetration and accelerating rate calorimetry (ARC) tests verify the exceptional safety of the pouch cells. By linking molecular microenvironment regulation to macroscopic battery safety, this work illuminates a viable pathway toward the commercialization of intrinsically safe SIBs.

item.title: From Order to Disorder: A Crystalline-Amorphous Core-Shell Structure Enables Superior Ionic Conductivity and Interfacial Stability in Halide Electrolytes
item.description: Halide solid-state electrolytes are critical for developing high-safety, high-energy-density all-solid-state lithium batteries. However, most existing synthesis methods for halide electrolytes rely on non-equilibrium strategies, which struggle to simultaneously achieve high ionic conductivity and good stability. Here, we propose a facile one-step solid-state route that constructs a highly conductive and structurally robust crystalline-amorphous core-shell heterostructure by aliovalent doping of Hf 4+ /Zr 4+ into Li 3 YCl 6 . In this heterostructure, the ordered crystalline core serves as a robust scaffold, while nanocrystallites that simultaneously promote structural integrity and ion transport are embedded within the continuous, highly conductive amorphous shell. These structural features synergistically establish a three-dimensional ion migration network with low transport barriers and high connectivity, enabling Li 2.6 Y 0.6 Hf 0.4 Cl 6 to achieve a room-temperature ionic conductivity of 1.4 mS·cm −1 , a 37-fold enhancement over the pristine phase, and an activation energy of 0.30 eV. Benefiting from its excellent interfacial stability against Li–In anode, all-solid-state batteries employing the LiNi 0.8 Mn 0.1 Co 0.1 O 2 cathode operate stably without a sulfide interlayer, achieving 80.8% capacity retention after 200 cycles at room temperature and 73.8% retention after 100 high-rate cycles at elevated temperature. With an additional sulfide interlayer to further optimize the interface, the cell delivers a prolonged cycle life with 87.2% capacity retention over 580 cycles. Through a straightforward solid-state doping approach, this work designs a highly conductive and structurally stable halide electrolyte, offering a new design paradigm for halide electrolytes.

item.title: Harnessing Li‐Ion Binding Energy for Solvation‐Guided Electrolyte Additive Design and Robust Solid Electrolyte Interphase Reinforcement
item.description: ABSTRACT The rational design of electrolyte systems is essential for stabilizing the electrode−electrolyte interface to enhance the electrochemical performance of lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs). Although conventional strategies focus on the introduction of specific functional moieties, the correlation between the molecular structure of an electrolyte additive and the extent of effective localized enrichment at the interface remains poorly understood. Herein, we propose a solvation‐guided additive design strategy in which the Li‐ion binding energy of the additive serves as a factor for effective solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) reinforcement. This hypothesis is validated by employing a σ‐bonding‐insulation‐based model system, which contains allyl methyl sulfone (AMS), allyl methyl carbonate (AMC), and allyl methyl ether (AME) as electrolyte additives with varying Li‐ion binding affinities. Computational simulations and spectroscopic analyses confirmed that AMS, which has the highest binding energy, preferentially participates in the Li‐ion solvation shell. This affinity, which facilitates the spontaneous migration of the additive toward the negative electrode during the SEI formation step, results in the development of a robust SEI layer concentrated at the negative electrode. These findings highlight the importance of interactions between Li‐ions and additives in interface engineering and provide a systematic framework for the development of high‐performance electrolyte additives.

item.title: Zwitterionic Thermoplastic Polyurethane‐Based Quasi‐Solid Polymer Electrolytes for Lithium Metal Batteries With Machine‐Learning‐Assisted Mechanistic Insights
item.description: ABSTRACT This study presents a quasi‐solid‐state electrolyte based on zwitterionic thermoplastic polyurethane (QS‐Z‐TPU) for lithium metal batteries. Unlike conventional quasi‐solid polymer electrolytes that mainly serve as passive liquid‐electrolyte reservoirs, QS‐Z‐TPU is designed as an active ion‐regulating matrix via phosphorylcholine‐derived zwitterionic groups in the TPU framework. The resulting electrolyte combines the elasticity and film‐forming capability of TPU with dual‐site ion regulation, where phosphate sites coordinate Li + while quaternary ammonium and urethane N‐H groups immobilize TFSI − anions. This design enhances electrolyte affinity while suppressing destructive swelling due to ionic crosslinking. QS‐Z‐TPU exhibits high ionic conductivity, a wide electrochemical stability window, and an enhanced Li + transference number. Machine‐learning‐assisted molecular modeling further reveals that the zwitterionic oligomer stabilizes separated LiTFSI configurations through cooperative Li + coordination and TFSI − association, substantially reducing the energetic penalty for ion‐pair separation. This regulated ion environment promotes uniform Li + flux at the lithium metal interface and facilitates the formation of a stable inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphase. Consequently, QS‐Z‐TPU enables stable Li plating/stripping and improves the cycling stability and rate capability of LFP|Li full cells, further validated in flexible pouch‐cell demonstrations. These findings highlight zwitterionic molecular engineering as an effective strategy for interface‐stabilizing quasi‐solid electrolytes.
